title: The Card Numbered 108: Villa Crespo, the Cooperative, and the Flower on the Silent Piano
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Villa Crespo, the House Where the Flute Was Kept

stops.name: Villa Crespo, the third son of a shoemaker who played flute
stops.date_confidence: attested; both Wikipedias give 2 December 1905. The coordinate is the Plazoleta Osvaldo Pugliese in Villa Crespo, which Spanish Wikipedia places a few metres from the birth house; the house itself has no recorded address.
stops.campa: On the second of December, in the barrio of Villa Crespo, Adolfo Pugliese and Aurelia Terragno have a son and name him Osvaldo Pedro. The father works in the shoe trade and plays the flute for his own pleasure; the two older boys, Adolfo Salvador Vicente, called Fito, and Alberto Roque, take up the violin. The barrio is tenements, workshops, Italian and Jewish immigrants, and music played on whatever a household can afford. Ninety years later a hearse will come back up these streets carrying him, driving against the traffic.
suggested_refs: The Plazoleta Osvaldo Pugliese and its monument, Villa Crespo, raised beside the birth house

stops.name: Villa Crespo, the father changes the instrument
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the switch to piano is attested in his own 1981 interview but no year is given, and the date here only orders the segment between his birth and his 1920 debut.
stops.campa: The boy is set to the violin first, like his brothers, and does badly at it. His father, who has heard him pick out melodies by ear, changes the instrument. From then on the piano is the assignment and then the trade. He studies with Antonio D'Agostino; other accounts add Vicente Scaramuzza and Pedro Rubione, and the sources do not agree on which of them taught him what. Around 1918 he leaves primary school to work, in a print shop among other places, and keeps at the keyboard in the hours the work leaves free.
stops.quote: tenés que aprender a tocar el piano
stops.quote_source: Osvaldo Pugliese quoting his father, interviewed by Mona Moncalvillo, Revista Humor Nº 59, May 1981, pp. 62-68, reprinted at elhistoriador.com.ar
suggested_refs: The 1981 Revista Humor interview, his fullest first-person account of the household
sources: Mona Moncalvillo interview, Revista Humor Nº 59, May 1981, via elhistoriador.com.ar

stops.name: Café de la Chancha, the trio at fifteen
stops.date_confidence: traditional; Spanish Wikipedia gives the venue and the age but no month, and the bar's address was never recorded. The coordinate is a Villa Crespo approximation, not a located door.
stops.campa: At fifteen he takes his first paid work as a musician, at a bar the barrio calls the Café de la Chancha, in a trio with the bandoneonist Domingo Faillac and the violinist Alfredo Ferrito. Nobody writes down the address; the place survives only in the nickname people gave it. Bandoneon, violin and piano: the standard three for a room with space for no more. Asked sixty years later when he started, he gives two numbers and no anecdote. The pay is coins, the audience is men coming in off a shift, and the barrio outside has somebody practising behind every second doorway.
stops.quote: Empecé a los 14 y tengo 75 años
stops.quote_source: Osvaldo Pugliese, interviewed by Mona Moncalvillo, Revista Humor Nº 59, May 1981, reprinted at elhistoriador.com.ar
suggested_refs: The Café de la Chancha, Villa Crespo, site unlocated
sources: Mona Moncalvillo interview, Revista Humor Nº 59, May 1981, via elhistoriador.com.ar

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the classical training underneath
stops.date_confidence: inferred; the teachers are named in both Wikipedias but with no dates, no addresses, and no agreement on the combination. The date orders the segment only.
stops.campa: The training underneath the tango is classical. He works the conservatory repertoire and the conservatory exercises while the dance halls pay him for something else entirely, and he never treats the two as separate schools. The boy who began by picking out melodies by ear is by now reading whatever is put in front of him. Which masters taught him what is reported differently by different sources: Antonio D'Agostino, Vicente Scaramuzza, Pedro Rubione, in combinations no two accounts share. No address for the instruction is recorded anywhere reachable.
stops.quote: Yo empecé con la música clásica; a mi padre y hermanos les gustaba la música y yo comencé tocando de oído.
stops.quote_source: Osvaldo Pugliese, interviewed by Mona Moncalvillo, Revista Humor Nº 59, May 1981, reprinted at elhistoriador.com.ar
suggested_refs: Vicente Scaramuzza's Buenos Aires piano school, named among his teachers in some accounts
sources: Mona Moncalvillo interview, Revista Humor Nº 59, May 1981

stops.name: Buenos Aires, 'Recuerdo' published under his father's name
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year of composition and publication; the reason for the paternal credit is disputed, with Spanish Wikipedia's article on the tango listing several competing explanations and no way to choose between them.
stops.campa: At eighteen he writes 'Recuerdo,' a tango he says he worked out on the tram between jobs. He will keep it in his own orchestra's book for the next seventy years. The sheet music published in 1924 carries the name Adolfo Pugliese, his father, and Julio De Caro's orchestra records it in 1926 under that name. Why the credit went to the father is disputed: that the son was too young to hold the rights, that the family needed the money, that he simply made his father a present of it. He was eighteen and not a minor. Nothing in the record chooses between the three.
suggested_refs: The 1924 sheet music of 'Recuerdo,' credited to A. Pugliese
Julio De Caro's 1926 recording

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Pollet's quartet and Firpo's orchestra
stops.date_confidence: traditional; Spanish Wikipedia dates the Pollet engagement to 1924 with no corroboration, one background account puts it in 1921, and tango.idoneos.com gives Firpo in 1926. Month arbitrary.
stops.campa: He is a hired pianist now, moving between the orchestras that keep the cafés and cabarets supplied: Enrique Pollet's quartet, then Roberto Firpo's orchestra, one of the oldest working names in the music. The pay is by the night. From inside the section he learns how a tango is held together at the bottom and how an orchestra breathes. He also learns which directors deal fairly with the men they hire. The dates are unstable: Spanish Wikipedia puts the Pollet engagement in 1924, a background account puts it in 1921, and tango.idoneos.com gives Firpo in 1926.
suggested_refs: Roberto Firpo's orchestra, the surviving link to the guardia vieja

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the piano chair in Pedro Maffia's sexteto
stops.date_confidence: attested by todotango and tango.idoneos.com for 1927; Spanish Wikipedia's 1926 is the outlier and is not followed here. Month unknown, defaulted.
stops.campa: Pedro Maffia, bandoneonist of the school Julio De Caro's sextet made, takes him into his own group. todotango and tango.idoneos.com date the engagement to 1927; Spanish Wikipedia says 1926 and stands alone in saying it. This is the tango that thinks: written arrangements, counter-melodies in the violins, a rhythm section that can drop to a whisper and come back on the beat. Pugliese is twenty-one, and he sits at the piano of one of the most demanding ensembles working in the city.
suggested_refs: Pedro Maffia's sexteto, and the decarean line it carried

stops.name: Café Nacional, the sextet with Vardaro and the tour that fails
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year and the outcome; the street number of this earlier Café Nacional is not confirmed, so the coordinate reuses the later documented Avenida Corrientes 960 site.
stops.campa: He leaves Maffia's group with the violinist Elvino Vardaro to lead a sextet of their own. Vardaro is the most admired bow in the city and will spend his life in ensembles that are remembered better than they were paid. Nobody standing behind this one holds capital. The Buenos Aires debut goes well; then they take it out to the provinces, and the tour loses money town by town until there is no ensemble left to bring home. Ten years on, when he builds an orchestra with his own name on it, he will not build it on this footing. Spanish Wikipedia is the only source for any of it. He is twenty-four.
suggested_refs: The Vardaro-Pugliese sextet, remembered as the most advanced ensemble of its moment and the shortest lived

stops.name: Buenos Aires, six in the evening to six in the morning
stops.date_confidence: attested as a condition, undated as an event; his own 1981 account names the hours but gives no year. Dated here to the middle of the decade's crisis to order the segment.
stops.campa: The work that pays is the cabaret, and the cabaret runs its musicians from six in the evening until six in the morning, seven nights, at whatever the house decides to pay. He is not yet thirty and has already been in three orchestras that folded. The crisis of the decade makes the terms worse and makes the men easier to replace. Playing those shifts with his back to the dancers, Pugliese starts talking to the others in the pit about what the arrangement actually is. He gives the hours in an interview forty-five years afterwards and never says which year, or which room.
stops.quote: nosotros trabajábamos como en un feudo, desde las seis de la tarde a las seis de la mañana
stops.quote_source: Osvaldo Pugliese, interviewed by Mona Moncalvillo, Revista Humor Nº 59, May 1981, reprinted at elhistoriador.com.ar
suggested_refs: The cabarets of the Buenos Aires centre in the 1930s, and their terms of employment
sources: Mona Moncalvillo interview, Revista Humor Nº 59, May 1981, via elhistoriador.com.ar

stops.name: Buenos Aires, affiliate number five of the musicians' union
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year and for his membership number by Spanish Wikipedia; the founding address is not recorded, so the coordinate is a generic downtown pin. Month unknown, defaulted.
stops.campa: He pushes for a union of popular musicians and becomes affiliate number five of the Sindicato Argentino de Músicos. The first strike wins a single day off and a four in the morning finish, which is to say two hours of the night handed back to men who had none. No address survives for the founding, and no minutes of the meeting that called it. From this year forward he is a man with a police file, opened before any government has a reason to care what a pianist thinks about anything.
stops.quote: ... donde el trabajo sea una dignidad personal y no un castigo
stops.quote_source: Osvaldo Pugliese, quoted in Horacio Tarcus, dir., Diccionario biográfico de la izquierda argentina (Emecé, 2007), p. 532, via Spanish Wikipedia; the Tarcus volume itself was not consulted directly
suggested_refs: The founding of the Sindicato Argentino de Músicos, 1935
sources: Mona Moncalvillo interview, Revista Humor Nº 59, May 1981, via elhistoriador.com.ar

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the card numbered 108
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year and the number by Spanish Wikipedia; the marriage to María Concepción Florio is given for the same year by English Wikipedia alone and is carried here as reconstruction. Month unknown, defaulted.
stops.campa: He joins the Communist Party of Argentina and is handed card number 108. The party in this country is small and one hundred and eight is a low number, and the number becomes a relic in the retelling. He will hold the card for fifty-nine years, through proscription, censorship and jail, and will never trade it for the career available to a bandleader who drops it. The same year, on the word of one encyclopedia and no other, he marries María Concepción Florio. The record preserves her name and two dates.
suggested_refs: Membership card no. 108, Partido Comunista de la Argentina

stops.name: Café Germinal, the sextet on Avenida Corrientes
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year, the venue and the personnel by Spanish Wikipedia; the street number of the Café Germinal is not recorded, so the coordinate is a generic Avenida Corrientes pin. Month arbitrary.
stops.campa: He puts a sextet on the stand at the Café Germinal on Avenida Corrientes, with the bandoneonists Alfredo Calabró, Juan Abelardo Fernández and Marcos Madrigal. The street number was never written down. He has the players and he has the arrangements; the sound he is working toward is not there yet, and this ensemble does not hold together long enough to find it. Corrientes at this hour is a street of cafés with orchestras inside them, one every block or two, and the audience walks from door to door making its comparisons out loud on the pavement.
suggested_refs: Café Germinal, Avenida Corrientes, one of the orchestra cafés of the 1930s

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the birth of Beba
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year by English Wikipedia; no month or day given, and no birth address. Coordinate is a generic Buenos Aires pin.
stops.campa: His daughter Lucela Delma is born and is called Beba from the beginning. She is the only child of the marriage, and she is born into a house where the orchestra rehearses in the front room. She takes the piano, as the household expects, and makes her own career on it, directing ensembles under her own name. She also becomes the keeper of her father's papers and his testimony. In 2010 she publishes 'Osvaldo Pugliese: testimonio de una vida' through JVE Ediciones. English Wikipedia gives the year of her birth and nothing else about it.
suggested_refs: Lucela Delma 'Beba' Pugliese, Osvaldo Pugliese: testimonio de una vida (JVE Ediciones, 2010), catalogued in Open Library

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the first detention
stops.date_confidence: attested by English Wikipedia as occurring shortly before the August debut, connected to the inauguration of a Communist Party headquarters; no exact date, no police record, no station named. Month inferred from the sequence.
stops.campa: Days before his orchestra's debut the police take him in, reportedly over the opening of a Communist Party headquarters. The surviving account says he was treated with respect at the station and released. It is the first detention anyone can date, and it happens under a conservative government, six years before Juan Perón is elected to anything. Everything the legend will later say about who jailed this man and when has to be laid alongside that fact.
suggested_refs: The 1939 detention, earliest dated arrest in the record

stops.name: Café El Nacional, the orchestra constituted as a cooperative
stops.date_confidence: attested; the date, the venue and the debut personnel are corroborated across both Wikipedias and both background accounts.
stops.campa: On the eleventh of August the Orquesta Típica Osvaldo Pugliese debuts at the Café El Nacional on Avenida Corrientes: Enrique Alessio, Osvaldo Ruggiero and Eduardo Armengol on bandoneons, Amadeo Mandarino singing. It is constituted as a cooperative. Every man in it holds a share of the takings and a voice in the decisions, the director included, and no manager stands above the payroll. Both Wikipedias and both background accounts agree on the date, the room and the personnel. The arrangement lasts fifty-six years.
stops.quote: El otro, fue el sistema de la orquesta; por ser una cooperativa, todos peleaban por su subsistencia, no era sólo el director que peleaba por su nombre.
stops.quote_source: Osvaldo Pugliese, interviewed by Mona Moncalvillo, Revista Humor Nº 59, May 1981, reprinted at elhistoriador.com.ar
suggested_refs: Café El Nacional, Avenida Corrientes 960, where the cooperative began
sources: Mona Moncalvillo interview, Revista Humor Nº 59, May 1981

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the two syllables that name the orchestra
stops.date_confidence: contested: English Wikipedia gives 1946 and one background account gives 1943, and no source reachable here adjudicates. The 1946 date is followed as the independently checked figure. Month unknown, defaulted.
stops.campa: He writes 'La yumba,' which is less a tango than an instruction. Yum-ba: the two-part attack the whole orchestra plays as one body, the piano landing on it like a hammer and the bandoneons closing behind. Played, it is recognisable at four bars' distance from the back of any hall in the country. It becomes the orchestra's opening, its closing, its signature and finally its name in other people's mouths. The year is given as 1943 in one account and 1946 in another.
stops.quote: permanezco fiel a esa tendencia; si lo hago bien o mal, mala suerte
stops.quote_source: Osvaldo Pugliese, interviewed by Mona Moncalvillo, Revista Humor Nº 59, May 1981, reprinted at elhistoriador.com.ar
suggested_refs: 'La yumba,' the orchestra's signature composition

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the year that may have been a queue
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: this is the most widely repeated episode in his legend and the least documented. Spanish Wikipedia states he was persecuted and jailed in 1948 and in the same passage quotes Arturo Jauretche denying it. No arrest record, press clipping or contemporaneous account was found on either side.
stops.campa: The story everybody tells is that Perón's police jailed him in 1948 for six months, and that his orchestra played the whole season with a flower laid on the closed piano. Arturo Jauretche, who lived that decade at close range, said the whole thing was invented, that Pugliese had been standing in a queue at the police station to collect his identity card. No arrest record has been produced. No newspaper of the day has been produced. The encyclopedia prints the claim and the denial in the same paragraph.
stops.quote: Esos son bolazos, leyenda pura; había hecho cola para sacar la cédula y lo invitaron a tomar un café para garronearle unas entradas a la milonga, no más...
stops.quote_source: Arturo Jauretche, quoted in Enrique Medina, 'Perón, Pugliese, en tres palabras,' Página/12, 3 March 2009
suggested_refs: Enrique Medina, 'Perón, Pugliese, en tres palabras,' Página/12, 3 March 2009

stops.name: Club Atlético Palermo, the milongas of the banned decade
stops.date_confidence: attested for the decade and the venue; Spanish Wikipedia's article on the club independently confirms that it hosted the great tango orchestras of the fifties and the neighbourhood's first milongas. The year is arbitrary within the decade.
stops.campa: At Fitz Roy 2238 the club's restaurant takes the great orchestras of the fifties, his among them, and the barrio holds its first milongas in that room. He works the clubs and the neighbourhood halls through the decade because the radio is closing to him, and the orchestra reaches its full height in those years. The dancers come regardless, in numbers no broadcast schedule can affect, filling club rooms across the barrios for a band the government of the day would rather nobody heard. Which year is not recorded; the Spanish article on the club gives only the decade.
suggested_refs: Club Atlético Palermo, Fitz Roy 2238, Palermo Hollywood

stops.name: Cárcel de Villa Devoto, the six months that are dated
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: English Wikipedia alone gives a January to July 1955 imprisonment at Devoto. The Spanish-language biography does not carry it and no third source confirms the months. Carried as the most probable factual core of the undated 1948 story, not as settled fact.
stops.campa: One source, and only one, has him held at the Villa Devoto prison from January to July of 1955, six months, in the last stretch of Perón's second government. If it is right, this is the real half year that the 1948 story borrowed and misdated. The detail every version keeps is that he refused any special handling inside and took his turn with the mop and bucket in the corridors alongside the other detainees. Asked in 1981 to count his jailings, he answered that talking about it would be 'un problema de vanidad.'
stops.quote: Ahí no le digo nada, porque hablar de eso sería un problema de vanidad: el que está en una lucha con las ideas, tiene que saber las reglas del juego.
stops.quote_source: Osvaldo Pugliese, interviewed by Mona Moncalvillo, Revista Humor Nº 59, May 1981, reprinted at elhistoriador.com.ar
suggested_refs: The Cárcel de Villa Devoto, Buenos Aires
sources: Mona Moncalvillo interview, Revista Humor Nº 59, May 1981

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the bird that had stopped singing
stops.date_confidence: attested by Spanish Wikipedia that his first radio appearance after Perón's fall was the tango 'Ya no cantás, chingolo'; the station is not named, no date is given, and the song title rests on that single source. Month inferred from the September coup.
stops.campa: Perón falls in September and the airwaves open again to the men who were kept off them. On his first broadcast after the fall Pugliese plays 'Ya no cantás, chingolo,' an old tango about a bird that no longer sings, and the audience takes the point without assistance. He did not write it. He chose it, out of a repertoire of thousands, for the first thing his orchestra would put on the air after the proscription lifted. Which station carried the programme is not recorded anywhere reachable, and neither is the date, and the title itself rests on a single encyclopedia line.
suggested_refs: 'Ya no cantás, chingolo,' the tango chosen for the first post-Perón broadcast

stops.name: Port of Buenos Aires, the vapor París
stops.date_confidence: attested for April 1957 by Spanish Wikipedia and by six further Spanish-language articles on other detainees, all naming the vapor París; English Wikipedia's 1956 is the outlier and is not followed. The berth coordinate is an unsourced approximation.
stops.campa: In April, under the military government of the Revolución Libertadora, the sweep called Operación Cardenal takes the Communist Party's Central Committee and thousands of militants with it. The detainees are held aboard a ship in the harbour, the vapor París. Pugliese is among them. Two years after Devoto, a different government with the opposite politics, the same cell and the same card. English and Spanish sources disagree by a year on when this happened; six separate Spanish articles carry 1957.
suggested_refs: Operación Cardenal, April 1957, and the detention ship París

stops.name: Radio Splendid, the flower on the lid
stops.date_confidence: attested by English Wikipedia that the orchestra played Radio Splendid without him during the Operación Cardenal detention with a flower on the piano; the year is corrected to 1957, the species of flower and the occasion of the ritual are contested, and the exact day is invented here only to place it inside the detention.
stops.campa: His chair at Radio Splendid is empty and the orchestra plays without him with a flower laid on the piano lid. This is the image that outlives every other thing about him, and its details are contested. A red carnation in one account; a single rose in another, the idea of a bandoneonist's wife who thought one flower finer than a vase of them, set out before every performance rather than only during arrests, handed afterwards to someone in the audience. Página/12 has this practice generating the inflated jail stories rather than recording them. Whether the flower ever marked an arrest at all is left open.
stops.quote: fueron dos o tres, seguro una
stops.quote_source: Francisco García Jiménez on how many times Pugliese was actually taken to a police station, quoted in Enrique Medina, 'Perón, Pugliese, en tres palabras,' Página/12, 3 March 2009
suggested_refs: Enrique Medina, 'Perón, Pugliese, en tres palabras,' Página/12, 3 March 2009, citing the poet Juan José Ceselli on the flower

stops.name: Moscow, eighty cities in three months
stops.date_confidence: attested by English Wikipedia for the year and the scale; the itinerary is not itemised in any reachable source and Moscow stands here for eighty cities. Month unknown, defaulted.
stops.campa: The orchestra crosses into the Soviet Union and plays some eighty cities in three months, a scale of touring no other tango orchestra of the era attempts. The programme does not change for the audience. A típica from Buenos Aires, six bandoneons and four violins and a piano, in Russian halls in the year of Sputnik and the year the Cuban revolution takes Havana. He is the guest of a state that regards him as one of its own. Which eighty cities they played is written down nowhere that can be reached.
suggested_refs: The 1959 Soviet tour of the Orquesta Típica Osvaldo Pugliese

stops.name: Beijing, twenty-eight cities in a month
stops.date_confidence: attested by English Wikipedia as part of the same 1959 trip; no dates, no venues, no itinerary. The month is inferred as following the Soviet leg.
stops.campa: From the Soviet Union the tour continues into China: twenty-eight cities in a single month, which is a city every day with the travelling done in between. The same repertoire, the same bandoneons, in front of audiences with no dancers on the floor and no reference at all for the music being played at them. Ten years earlier this orchestra was working neighbourhood clubs because the radio would not have it. Of the Chinese leg nothing survives in any reachable source except the count of cities and the count of days.
suggested_refs: The 1959 China tour, undocumented beyond its arithmetic

stops.name: Buenos Aires, 'Milonga para Fidel'
stops.date_confidence: attested for the title and the year by both Wikipedias; no month, and no record of any contact between Pugliese and the Cuban government at the time of writing.
stops.campa: He writes 'Milonga para Fidel' for a revolution two years old. He has never met Fidel Castro and there is no correspondence between them; the piece is a declaration made from a piano in Buenos Aires, in the only form the country has given him for saying such things out loud. Cuba does not forget it, and will decorate him by order of its Council of State thirty-one years later. He is fifty-five and has been in the party for twenty-five years. The piece is titled with the man's first name and nothing else.
suggested_refs: 'Milonga para Fidel,' 1961

stops.name: Buenos Aires, ten recordings a year
stops.date_confidence: attested as a fact, undated as an event: English Wikipedia gives no year for the ban, only Onganía's government. Onganía held power from June 1966 to June 1970, so the measure belongs in that range and the date here is its opening.
stops.campa: Juan Carlos Onganía's government bars him from radio broadcasts and from public places and restricts the orchestra to ten recordings a year. No source gives the date of the order; the general governs from June 1966 to June 1970, and it falls somewhere inside that. He is sixty-one, at the head of the most popular orchestra in the country, and formally not broadcastable in it. He keeps playing the clubs, as he did in the fifties, on the same terms.
stops.quote: Nadie puede luchar contra el sentimiento del pueblo, y la soberanía nacional no sólo se defiende con la armas, sino también con la cultura…
stops.quote_source: Osvaldo Pugliese, interviewed by Mona Moncalvillo, Revista Humor Nº 59, May 1981, reprinted at elhistoriador.com.ar; the typographical error is the source page's
suggested_refs: The Onganía dictatorship's broadcasting prohibitions, 1966-1970
sources: Mona Moncalvillo interview, Revista Humor Nº 59, May 1981

stops.name: Tokyo, one hundred and thirty-five performances
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year and the count by English Wikipedia, corroborated by both background accounts; no venues are named and Tokyo stands for the whole tour. Month unknown, defaulted.
stops.campa: The orchestra plays Japan for the first time: one hundred and thirty-five performances across five months. Japanese collectors have been buying Argentine records for decades and know the arrangements bar by bar, some of them better than the dancers at home. Five months is a long time to keep a cooperative on the road, and every man is paid out of the same shares abroad as at home. The audience built here is still buying the recordings a generation after his death. No venue is named in any reachable source, and no Japanese city but Tokyo. He returns in 1979 and again in 1989.
suggested_refs: The Japanese tango audience and its Argentine record collections

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the widower
stops.date_confidence: attested for both years by English Wikipedia and by nothing else; the marriage to Lydia Elman in 1972 is single-sourced and carried as reconstruction. No months are given for either event.
stops.campa: María Concepción Florio dies after thirty-five years of marriage. He marries Lydia Elman the following year. The record of both women is a line each on an encyclopedia page, and only one page carries either: no account of either life, no ceremony described, no address. He says nothing about either marriage in the long interview he gives ten years afterwards. What is documented from this decade is a touring schedule, kept up by a man approaching seventy, with the shares still divided the way they were divided in 1939 and a daughter of thirty-two working as a pianist in the same city.
suggested_refs: The gap in the record around both marriages

stops.name: Olivos, the three words at the residence
stops.date_confidence: attested that a meeting took place after Perón's return; the wording is contested, English Wikipedia giving an apology for pending matters and Página/12 giving three words at Olivos. The coordinate is the presidential residence at Olivos, named by Página/12 but with no room specified. Month unknown, defaulted.
stops.campa: Perón is back in the country and back in the presidency, and the bandleader his governments proscribed is invited out to the residence at Olivos among the artists. What passes between them is reported two ways. English-language sourcing has Perón apologising for the small matters left pending between them; the Buenos Aires account gives three words at the door. Either way it is Perón who asks. The version that circulates hardest, praising Pugliese for knowing how to forgive, has the direction backwards.
stops.quote_source: Juan Perón to Osvaldo Pugliese at Olivos, 1973, as given in Enrique Medina, 'Perón, Pugliese, en tres palabras,' Página/12, 3 March 2009
suggested_refs: Enrique Medina, 'Perón, Pugliese, en tres palabras,' Página/12, 3 March 2009

stops.name: Bogotá, the Colombian tour
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year by English Wikipedia; no cities, venues or dates are itemised, and Bogotá stands for the country. Month unknown, defaulted.
stops.campa: The orchestra tours Colombia. In Colombia the tango is not foreign music: the country has held it since Carlos Gardel's aeroplane burned at Medellín in 1935, and it is played in cantinas that never saw a Buenos Aires dance floor. Pugliese is seventy-four and travelling with a dozen men and their instruments, which is what the cooperative has always been, a payroll that exists only while it is working. No venue for the Colombian dates is recorded.
suggested_refs: The Colombian tango audience, and the 1935 Medellín crash

stops.name: Havana, the festival and the camera
stops.date_confidence: attested by Spanish Wikipedia for the festival and the documentary; English Wikipedia lists Cuban tours in 1984, 1988 and 1992 while one background account gives only 1992, so the spacing of his Cuban visits is uncertain. Month unknown, defaulted.
stops.campa: He goes to Havana for the International Tango Festival, and the trip is filmed for the Argentine-Cuban documentary 'Tango y Tango.' The island has had his sheet music since 1961 and now gets the man. He is seventy-eight, and the repertoire he brings is half a century old and unaltered in its principles: the same attack, the same shares, the same director sitting at the piano rather than standing in front of it with a baton. Sources disagree over how many times he went to Cuba, giving 1984, 1988 and 1992 in one list and only 1992 in another.
suggested_refs: 'Tango y Tango,' Argentine-Cuban documentary filmed at the Havana festival

segments.name: The Colón, and the Honors of Other Countries

stops.name: Teatro Colón, the house that was kept for opera
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date and the venue by both Wikipedias and both background accounts. English Wikipedia gives five standing ovations; the crowd figure of 5,000 and the ten-minute ovation that circulate elsewhere are unsourced and exceed the house's capacity, and are not carried here. The line that his mother had wanted this and did not live to see it is [R]: carried from a background account, untraced to any primary source, kept on the operator's ruling.
stops.campa: On the twenty-sixth of December, three weeks past his eightieth birthday, he leads the orchestra onto the stage of the Teatro Colón at Cerrito 628, the house built for opera and kept for it. His mother had wanted this and did not live to see it. The audience stands five times. Larger figures for the crowd and longer ones for the ovation circulate freely and rest on nothing; what the record gives is five ovations and an eighty-year-old man at the piano.
suggested_refs: Teatro Colón, Cerrito 628, Buenos Aires

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Ciudadano Ilustre
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year by both Wikipedias; no ceremony date or venue is recorded, so the coordinate is a generic city pin. The Konex and Academia dates are attested separately by Spanish Wikipedia.
stops.campa: The City of Buenos Aires declares him Ciudadano Ilustre. Inside living memory and by written order, the same city forbade him to appear in public places in it, and he holds now the card he held then. The Fundación Konex gave him its platinum award for orchestra direction the year before and will give him two more, the last of them ten years after his death; the Academia Nacional del Tango makes him an honorary academic in 1990. For the citizenship itself no ceremony date and no address are recorded, only the year.
stops.quote: el tango va a salir adelante como nuestro país, porque tienen reservas
stops.quote_source: Osvaldo Pugliese, interviewed by Mona Moncalvillo, Revista Humor Nº 59, May 1981, reprinted at elhistoriador.com.ar
suggested_refs: The Ciudadano Ilustre distinction of the City of Buenos Aires, 1986

stops.name: Teatro Solís, the other city that claims the music
stops.date_confidence: attested by English Wikipedia for a Uruguayan tour with a Montevideo appearance at the Solís; no date or programme is given. Month unknown, defaulted.
stops.campa: Across the river, at the Teatro Solís in Montevideo, the orchestra plays for the other city that claims the tango and has as good a title to it. Montevideo and Buenos Aires have argued the paternity of the music for eighty years and have bought the same records throughout the argument. The Solís is Montevideo's opera house, which makes this the second such stage to open to him in two years. He is eighty-one and still directing from the bench, hands flat on the keys, giving the attack with his shoulders.
suggested_refs: Teatro Solís, Montevideo

stops.name: France, Commandeur des Arts et des Lettres
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year and the rank by both Wikipedias; whether the insignia was conferred in Paris or at the French embassy in Buenos Aires is not stated, and the Paris coordinate stands for the honouring state rather than a located ceremony.
stops.campa: France makes him Commandeur de l'Ordre des Arts et des Lettres. The republic is decorating a Communist Party member of fifty-two years' standing who has been banned from the air by two Argentine governments of opposite colours, held on a ship in his own harbour, and possibly imprisoned for six months at Devoto. He toured France four years earlier. Where the insignia changes hands, in Paris or at the embassy in Buenos Aires, no source consulted will say.
suggested_refs: Ordre des Arts et des Lettres, grade of Commandeur, 1988

stops.name: Avenida Corrientes 960, the plaque at fifty years
stops.date_confidence: attested by Spanish Wikipedia for the plaque and the anniversary; the day is inferred from the 11 August 1939 debut it commemorates, not stated by the source.
stops.campa: A plaque goes up on Avenida Corrientes for the fifty years since the orchestra was founded at that address. The Café El Nacional itself is gone, as most of the orchestra cafés are gone, the street having turned to cinemas and bookshops that stay open all night. He is alive to stand under his own commemorative bronze, which is an unusual arrangement for a musician and unusual for this street, most of whose plaques went up for the dead. Fifty years earlier three bandoneonists and a singer opened with him here for a share of the door. It is also the route his coffin will take.
suggested_refs: The commemorative plaque at Avenida Corrientes 960

stops.name: Amsterdam, the Carré with Piazzolla's sextet
stops.date_confidence: attested that the two ensembles shared a bill at the Koninklijk Theater Carré in June 1989; English Wikipedia's Piazzolla article gives 26 June and its Pugliese article gives 29 June, and the discrepancy is not resolved here.
stops.campa: At the Koninklijk Theater Carré on the Amstel, the orchestra shares a bill with Ástor Piazzolla's sextet, seventy years after a fifteen-year-old took his first paid work at the Café de la Chancha. Piazzolla spent a career being told he had destroyed the tango; Pugliese spent his being kept off the radio for his politics. They play the same Dutch circus theatre on the same night, both of them old. The sources give two different dates in the same week for it.
suggested_refs: Koninklijk Theater Carré, Amstel 115-125, Amsterdam

stops.name: Havana, the Alejo Carpentier Medal
stops.date_confidence: attested for the exact date and the awarding body by English Wikipedia.
stops.campa: On the eleventh of November Cuba's Council of State awards him the Alejo Carpentier Medal. He is eighty-six and it is the last foreign honour he will collect in person. The milonga he wrote for Fidel Castro is thirty-one years old. In the interval he has outlived the government that put him on a ship in his own harbour and the government that would not let him near a microphone, and the argument about whether he was ever really imprisoned is still running. He has changed his position on nothing.
suggested_refs: The Alejo Carpentier Medal, conferred by the Cuban Council of State, 11 November 1992

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the twenty-fifth of July
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date and the cause by both Wikipedias; the hospital or house where he died is not named in any reachable source.
stops.campa: He dies in Buenos Aires on the twenty-fifth of July, eighty-nine years old, after a short illness. Where exactly is not recorded. The cooperative founded at the Café El Nacional in August 1939 has outlasted every commercially managed orchestra of its generation, fifty-six years of shared takings and shared votes, three generations of bandoneonists passing through the same chairs, and it does not survive him as a working body. He had been directing to the end of his strength. His daughter is a pianist. His card is still number 108.
suggested_refs: The obituaries of July 1995 in the Buenos Aires press

stops.name: Palacio de la Legislatura, lying in state
stops.date_confidence: attested by Spanish Wikipedia that the body lay in state at the Concejo Deliberante; the coordinate is the Palacio de la Legislatura at Perú 130, its seat until 1995. The day is inferred from the death date.
stops.campa: His body lies in state at Perú 130, in the palace that housed the city's Concejo Deliberante, which is where Buenos Aires puts the dead it has decided belong to it. Nine years earlier the same city made him one of its illustrious citizens; before that it had forbidden him public places. The queue is the ordinary queue of a popular musician's funeral here: dancers, bandoneonists, men and women who paid at the door of the club dances for forty years and never met him, standing in a July cold along Perú and around into Diagonal Sur.
suggested_refs: Palacio de la Legislatura, Perú 130, seat of the Concejo Deliberante until 1995
sources: Spanish Wikipedia, 'Palacio de la Legislatura de la Ciudad de Buenos Aires'

stops.name: Avenida Corrientes, the cortege against the traffic
stops.date_confidence: attested by Spanish Wikipedia for the route and its direction; no hour is recorded and the day is inferred from the death date.
stops.campa: The hearse goes up Avenida Corrientes the wrong way, against the flow, the whole length of the street where he played the Nacional and the Germinal and where the plaque went up six years earlier. The traffic is stopped for it. Driving the wrong way up Corrientes is not a procedure any funeral is entitled to, and it was granted anyway. He had worked this street since 1929, first as a hired pianist in other men's orchestras and then for fifty-six years at the head of his own. No hour is recorded for the cortege, and no account of who authorised the route.
suggested_refs: The contra-flow funeral cortege along Avenida Corrientes, July 1995

stops.name: Cementerio de la Chacarita, the mausoleum paid for by strangers
stops.date_confidence: attested for the burial, the sculptor and the completion year by English Wikipedia; the coordinate is the cemetery as located by OpenStreetMap, and the grave's exact plot is not given. Month unknown, defaulted.
stops.campa: He is buried at Chacarita. Two years later a mausoleum designed by Juan Carlos Ferraro is finished over the grave, paid for by contributions from admirers in Argentina and abroad, which is the same arrangement the orchestra ran on: everyone puts in, nobody owns it. The cemetery is fifteen minutes' walk from the barrio he was born in and holds most of the tango dead of the century. Which plot is his is not given in any reachable source, and no account of the visits says which flower. Visitors leave flowers on the stone.
suggested_refs: The Pugliese mausoleum at Chacarita, by Juan Carlos Ferraro, completed 1997

stops.name: Malabia station, the name added to the line
stops.date_confidence: contested: the Spanish Wikipedia article on the station dates the renaming to a 2009 law, while the article on Pugliese and ecured.cu both say from 2011, most likely the year of implementation. Month unknown, defaulted.
stops.campa: After years of petitioning by neighbours, the city legislates that the Line B underground station at Corrientes and Malabia, in the barrio where he was born, carry his name: Malabia - Osvaldo Pugliese. The law is dated 2009 and other sources date the change to 2011, which is probably the year the signage was actually swapped. Villa Crespo also has a plazoleta and a monument to him, standing a few metres from the house where he was born and a short walk from the bar where he was first paid to play. Every train on the line now announces his name, forty-odd times a day, to people going to work.
suggested_refs: Estación Malabia - Osvaldo Pugliese, Línea B, Av. Corrientes 5300

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the name said before the amplifiers
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the invocation is widely attested as a living practice and English Wikipedia repeats the Charly García origin story, but nothing dates its beginning. The date only places the stop last in the segment and asserts nothing.
stops.campa: Argentine musicians invoke him against technical disaster: his photograph taped inside an instrument case, his name said aloud before the amplifiers are switched on, San Pugliese. The origin usually given is a Charly García concert at which nothing worked until a Pugliese record was put through the system. No church canonised him and the joke is entirely serious. He was a saint of nothing. He paid his musicians in shares and would not give up a party card.
suggested_refs: The San Pugliese invocation among Argentine musicians, and the Charly García concert given as its origin
